summary: Defines two YANG modules, ietf-system-capabilities and ietf-notification-capabilities. The first gives a place to report YANG-related capabilities of a server, at runtime or in an instance data file. The second adds capabilities for datastore update notification subscriptions described in RFC 8641.

eli5.summary: A device can publish a list of what it can do, and a second list for what updates it can announce.

questions: how to discover what a netconf server supports
how to find yang push capabilities of a device
subtitle: Two YANG modules that let a network device say, in a machine-readable way, what it can and cannot do.

tldr.problem: Network devices have capabilities that depend on the vendor and on deployment, such as which data can be reported on change. Management systems need to know these limits, both before a device is deployed and while it runs.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9196 defines ietf-system-capabilities, a placeholder structure that other modules augment with capabilities, and ietf-notification-capabilities, which uses it to describe the YANG-Push subscription limits of RFC 8641. The data can be read from a live server or shipped as a YANG instance data file.
tldr.outcome: A client can look up a capability for a datastore or even a single data node, with more specific entries overriding system-wide ones. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9196 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Capabilities Need Publishing
sections.content:
Servers and publishers often have capabilities: values that describe operational behavior and need to be conveyed to clients. The RFC calls this part of the API contract between server and client. Examples it gives are the maximum size of data that can be stored or transferred, and whether a node supports on-change telemetry.

The goal is a common format that is vendor independent, machine readable, and identical at implementation time and at runtime. Implementation-time information matters to makers of a Network Management System (NMS) and to system integrators, who would otherwise have to wait for a working network node to read the data from. Runtime information matters for purely model-driven applications such as a NETCONF browser, for capabilities that change (for example with licensing or hardware constraints), and for checking that earlier published information matches what was implemented.
sections.eli5: Before you buy a gadget you want to read what it can do, not wait until it is plugged in. This RFC gives gadgets a standard way to write that down, and to answer when asked.

sections.title: Implementation-Time and Runtime Information
sections.content:
The RFC defines two terms. Implementation-time information is about the server's behavior and is available from a source other than a running server. Runtime information is available from the running server through management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF.

Capabilities are represented as instance data based on one or more capability-defining YANG modules. For the implementation-time case, capabilities SHOULD be provided by the implementer as YANG instance data files complying with RFC 9195, retrievable without a live network node, for example from a product website. For the runtime case, capabilities SHOULD be available over NETCONF or RESTCONF from the live server. Implementations that can change capabilities at runtime SHOULD support on-change notifications about the system-capabilities container.
sections.eli5: There are two moments to ask: before the gadget exists in your house, by reading its spec sheet, and later, by asking the gadget itself. Both answers should look the same.

sections.title: The System Capabilities Module
sections.content:
The module ietf-system-capabilities contains no capabilities itself. It offers augmentation points where other modules add them. Every set of capabilities MUST be wrapped in a container, and those wrapper containers are augmented at /sysc:system-capabilities and at /sysc:system-capabilities/sysc:datastore-capabilities/sysc:per-node-capabilities. The data is read-only operational state.

A value can be set at the system level, at the datastore level, or for specific data nodes of a datastore together with their subtrees. A datastore-capabilities list is keyed by datastore name, and each entry holds a per-node-capabilities list whose entries select nodes with a node-selector. The special value / means all data nodes in the datastore. The solution works for both NMDA and non-NMDA servers; for non-NMDA servers, config false data is treated as part of the running datastore.

Only one specific datastore can be named per entry. The module description says the identity for conventional datastores must not be used, because it stands for a set of configuration datastores.
sections.eli5: It is an empty set of labelled drawers. Other documents decide what goes into the drawers: one for the whole device, one per storage area, and one for particular items.

sections.title: Finding a Capability Value
sections.content:
Values at more specific levels override less specific ones. The module spells out the lookup for a capability on a specific data node of a specific datastore:

  1. Find the datastore-capabilities entry for that datastore.
  2. If found, go through its per-node-capabilities entries in the order they appear. The first entry that specifies the capability and whose node-selector selects the node defines the value.
  3. If nothing was found and the capability is given under the system-capabilities container outside the list, use that value.
  4. Otherwise the system is not capable of providing a value, and its behavior is unspecified.

Because the first match wins, the system SHALL order entries by precedence, and the order MUST NOT change unless the capabilities change. Putting more specific matches before less specific ones gives longest-path matching.
sections.eli5: Check the note on the specific item first, then the note on its shelf, then the note on the whole store. The first note you find wins.

sections.title: YANG-Push Notification Capabilities
sections.content:
The module ietf-notification-capabilities augments the system capabilities with limits for YANG-Push, the datastore update subscriptions of RFC 8641. A publisher can send updates periodically or on change. The RFC explains why a publisher needs to say what it supports: some data, such as an in-octet counter, changes too often, other small changes are irrelevant, and some implementations simply cannot do on-change for a given object. Support for on-change in general does not mean it works for every node.

The subscription-capabilities container holds these leaves:

  • max-nodes-per-update: the maximum number of data nodes in an update, which helps avoid the update-too-big error.
  • periodic-notifications-supported: whether periodic notifications work for the selected nodes.
  • minimum-update-period or supported-update-period: the allowed periods, in centiseconds. A period that is not supported can give a period-unsupported error.
  • on-change-supported, minimum-dampening-period and supported-excluded-change-type: on-change support, the shortest dampening period, and which change types can be excluded. These depend on the on-change feature.

Support is expressed with the notification-support bits config-changes and state-changes, which cover config true and config false nodes. A minimum dampening period that is present and greater than zero implies dampening is mandatory. If one subscription covers nodes with different values, using a value acceptable for only some of them may get the subscription rejected.
sections.eli5: A news service can say how often it can send you updates, how many items fit in one message, and which topics it can announce the moment they change.

sections.title: Worked Instance Data Examples
sections.content:
The appendices show two instance data sets for hypothetical devices. The first, an acme-router, implements running and operational datastores. Every change can be reported on change from running, but from operational only config false nodes and some of that data can be. Interface statistics are not reported on change except for two counters, in-octets and out-octets, where a small dampening period is mandated.

The second, an acme-switch, implements running, candidate and operational datastores. Every change can be reported on change from running, nothing from candidate, and all config false data from operational. Periodic subscriptions are supported for running and operational but not candidate.
sections.eli5: The examples are two sample spec sheets, one for a pretend router and one for a pretend switch, showing which kinds of announcements each can make.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules define a schema for data reached via NETCONF, RESTCONF or instance data files. NETCONF's mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH and RESTCONF's is TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) can restrict which users see which content.

The RFC warns that capability values can leak useful information. Knowing the minimum update period of periodic subscriptions might, for example, tell an attacker how long unauthorized configuration changes could stay active before detection. Documents that augment these modules are encouraged to document the security considerations of their new nodes following BCP 216. All protocol-accessible data nodes here are read-only, and access control can hide data marked as sensitive. Instance data files should be protected using normal file-handling mechanisms.
sections.eli5: A list of what a device can do is also a list of what it cannot do, so you should only show it to people you trust.
